terms.def: To combine an element with oxygen or convert an element into its oxide. For example, when carbon burns, it combines with oxygen to form either carbon dioxide or carbon monoxide; iron combines with oxygen in the air to form an iron oxide commonly known as rust.

The word tensile refers to tension, or pulling apart. Tensile strength refers to the strength different materials display when placed under tension. In the Imperial system, tensile strength is measured in pounds per square inch (psi). In the metric system, tensile strength is measured in kilopascals (kPa) or newtons per square millimetre (N/mm2). The area referred to (square inches of mm2) is the cross-sectional area of the material.
Similar in meaning to the word pliable or ductile. A malleable substance is one capable of being shaped or formed by hammering or by rolling. A malleable material may be bent without breaking.
An alloy is a metal composed of two or more chemical elements, of which at least one is a metal.
The term is applied to metals or alloys that contain 5% or more of iron.
Pig iron is the basic metal obtained from iron ore. Most ferrous metals begin as pig iron. It has a very high carbon content (2.5% to 4.5%) and is cast into bars called pigs.

Soft, malleable metals can be made by alloying pig iron and nickel. The resulting metal is known as nodular iron. Wrought iron and ingot iron are two other soft, easily worked and relatively weak metals used for fabricating non-structural components.

Standard steel is an iron alloy containing manganese, carbon and/or other alloying elements. Standard steel is stronger and harder than the iron family, yet it is softer than tool steel. The carbon content affects the properties of steel. About 0.2% carbon makes a structural steel such as would be used for the framework of a skyscraper. Higher carbon content makes the steel harder. At 0.8% carbon the steel is suitable for making drills and hammers. At 1.0% carbon content you can make razor blades.

Steel with a high content of carbon is called tool steel. As the name implies, tool steel is used for making tools. It is hard enough to cut standard steel and iron. The metal must be able to withstand high temperatures, high load and abrasive conditions. Because of the many applications of tools, tool steels must vary in their composition.

As you have learned, steel itself is an alloy of iron and carbon, but a number of steels having many different elements alloyed with them can be grouped under the heading of alloy steels. Nickel, chromium, molybdenum, tungsten and vanadium may be added in amounts up to a total of about 5% to increase toughness or to increase strength at high temperatures.

One steel alloy which has some very special properties is stainless steel. It contains chromium and usually nickel, in amounts up to a total of 25%. Stainless steel has high tensile strength, ductility and hardness as well as being highly resistant to corrosion and oxidation.

Non-ferrous metals contain less than 5% iron and, in most cases, contain no iron at all. Examples of non-ferrous metals are aluminum, copper, zinc and lead. Included in this group of non-ferrous metals are alloys such as bronze and brass.

Aluminum is light weight and resistant to corrosion. It has low electrical resistance, high heat conductivity and good ductility combined with considerable strength. Used extensively in the A-3 aeronautical industry, aluminum is also used for cooking utensils, industrial tanks and vats, residential windows and doors, and electrical transmission lines.

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Zinc is cheaper than copper. Combining it with copper to form brass results in a metal that has improved properties over both copper and zinc. Brass is stronger than copper and is corrosive resistant making it ideal metal for ships’ fittings, locks, and boiler and condenser tubes. Standard brass, which contains 30 to 34% zinc, is used extensively for ornamental purposes, cabinet hardware, door and window hardware and plumbing valves.

the measuring and the marking or scribing of lines on materials out of which you are going to build something. Since these lines are taken from plans or drawings, layout involves the skill of transferring measurements or dimensions accurately and clearly.
scoring or marking a line on a hard or semi-hard surface with a sharp instrument.
The construction industry in Canada uses two systems of measurements: Imperial and metric.

In construction, the longest unit of Imperial measure is the yard. Yards are divided into three equal parts called feet. Feet are divided into twelve equal parts called inches. 1 yard = 3 feet 1 foot = 12 inches 1 yard = 36 inches

Inch Division Inches are divided into equal parts as illustrated in Figure 1. Fractions used in construction can be as large as 12" ; but for greater precision, quarters, eighths, sixteenths and so on are used. Most measuring operations in construction do not require accuracy beyond thirty-seconds of an inch. D-1-2

Metric measurements in construction are most often in metres or millimetres. Millimetres are illustrated in Figure 2. There are 1000 millimetres in one metre. Rather than use fractions, the metric system uses decimals. Therefore 2.360 m (metres) can also be written as 2360 mm (millimetres) by moving the decimal three places to the right.
The selection of a measuring device in construction is usually dictated by the length of the measurement to be taken and by the accuracy required.

Long flexible steel tapes as illustrated in Figure 3 are wound inside a convenient carrying case. Lengths range from 15 m to 60 m (50' to 200'). Long steel tapes are marked with graduations of two millimetres for metric tapes and eighths of an inch for Imperial tapes.

A shorter, spring-loaded steel tape ranging in length from 2 m to 7.5 m (6' to 25') is carried in the tool pouch or pocket of most construction workers. The pocket tape, as illustrated in Figure 4, is equipped with a small hook at the zero end of the tape. The hook should slide an amount equal to its own thickness to permit accurate internal and external measuring.

Pocket Tape The pocket tape is easy to use, accurate, long enough for most occasions, yet convenient to carry. Pocket tapes range in width from 12 mm, 19 mm to 25 mm (12", 3/4" and 1"). Wide blades are more rigid than narrow blades when extended; however, narrow blades are easier to carry in your pocket. Graduations are at one millimetre intervals on metric tapes, while Imperial tapes have markings at sixteenths and/or thirty-seconds of an inch. D-1: Identify Basic Measuring and Layout Tools for Construction D-1-3

There are two types of steel rules: one has the line of cord and the other does not. Both types are folded in half for convenience and are very flexible to follow curved lines. Line of cord is useful for reproducing angles from 1° to 120° in 12 ° increments. Use dividers to set the angle required on the line of cord scales; then set the dividers on the two pivot points thus reproducing the angle.

To ensure that layout lines and cuts are straight and square, construction workers may use a variety of squares. The three predominantly used are the framing square, the try square and the combination square. For best results with a square, you should ensure that the size of the square matches the size of the workpiece being laid out or checked for squareness.
Framing squares (Figure 5) measure 600 mm (2') on their long side and 400 mm (16") on their short side.
Framing Square To mark a layout line at 90° to the edge of a board, simply hook the long side over the edge of the board, and mark the face of the board along the short edge of the square (Figure 6).

Layout for a Square D-1-4 Various angles can be laid out with a framing square; for example, a 45° angle can be accurately laid out if you place the framing square so that the edge of a board intersects the sides of the framing square at an equal measurement along each side of the square (Figure 7).
Laying Out 45° D-1: Identify Basic Measuring and Layout Tools for Construction D-1-5

the measuring and marking of lines on materials out of which you are going to build something. Since these lines are taken from plans or drawings, layout involves the skill of transferring measurements or dimensions accurately and clearly.
Mechanics are required to use both metric and Imperial measuring systems in their normal workday; therefore, a good understanding of both systems is a must.

Inch Divisions Clearance between pistons and cylinder walls could be listed as 0.0032 inches. Measurements to such a high degree of accuracy are usually taken by special instruments such as dial indicators, micrometers or feeler gauges. D-3-2

Mechanics use the metric system of measurement to indicate bolt sizes, nut sizes, bolt length, piston diameter and length of piston stroke. The most common metric measurement used for the above examples is the millimetre (Figure 27). When a greater degree of accuracy is needed, mechanics use hundredths of a millimetre.

There are several styles of calipers used by mechanics to compare measurements of one item to another. Figure 28 illustrates inside calipers, outside calipers and straight-leg dividers. Inside calipers are used to compare inside measurements such as the diameters of holes or the space between two faces. Outside calipers are excellent for checking the diameter of cylindrical objects such as spindles, axles and shafts.
Calipers Dividers are used for layout only. They are never used to compare the inside measurement of one object to the outside measurement of another.

The scribers illustrated in Figure 29 are marking tools made with a hardened tempered steel scriber point that will mark mild steel and other relatively soft metals. They are precision tools that should not be abused by using them for any other purposes.
Scribers D-3: Identify Basic Measuring and Layout Tools for Mechanics D-3-3

The centre punch, illustrated in Figure 30, has a tapered bit with a broad, sharp point. It is used primarily for punching an indentation in a piece of metal as a guide for starting a drill bit. For example, you would first mark the part to be drilled with a scriber or pencil, and then place the centre punch directly on this mark. With a hammer, strike the head of the punch a good sharp blow. The indentation in the material will prevent the tip of the drill from slipping out of position, thus making it easier to start your drill.

Prick Punch The points of prick punches are ground to an included angle of 30°. This gives the prick punch a very thin point which makes it easy to see where you are placing the sharp point on a workpiece. But at the same time, this very thin point is fairly fragile and easily damaged if misused. Centre punches are ground to an included angle of 90°, making them far more durable, but the relatively blunt point is more difficult to exactly position on a smooth surface. D-3-4 D-4-1

The box end wrench shown in Figure 33 is an excellent tool for tightening and loosening nuts and bolts. Unlike the open-end wrench, the box-end wrench is made to grip the nut or bolthead on all sides. This prevents slipping and allows greater leverage. The opening for the nut or bolthead on the box-end wrench differs from that of the open-end wrench in that it is closed. This closed opening makes it necessary for the wrench to be slipped over the top of the nut or bolthead. The sharp edges or points around the inner circumference of the opening serve to grip the bolthead more securely.
As the name implies, the combination wrench (Figure 34) is an open-end wrench and a box- end wrench combined into one tool. Basically these wrenches are designed to turn bolts and/or nuts.

Combination Wrenches All the features of open-end and box-end wrenches apply also to a combination wrench and you will find it a very convenient tool. It has the speed of the open-end wrench for running a nut or bolt down snug and the strength of the box-end wrench for completely tightening a nut or bolt. Combination wrenches are available with offset heads, 6- or 12-point heads and in a wide selection of sizes and lengths. D-4: Identify Wrenches D-4-3

Adjustable Wrench The adjustable wrench (Figure 35) is very similar to the open-end wrench except that it has the provision for adjusting the opening to suit the nut or bolt being turned. The adjustable jaw is moved by a knurled nut which has a locking mechanism on some models. The size of all adjustable wrenches is designated by the wrench length, which varies from 4" to 24". For example, the 4" wrench has a 12" jaw capacity while the 12" wrench fits a nut 516 1- " across.

Adjustable wrenches are useful at times but should never be used as a substitute for an open- end or box-end wrench. Adjustable wrenches can be pulled in either direction for light loads but develop their greatest strength when pressure is applied to the side of the wrench with the fixed jaw as illustrated in Figure 36. Always be sure the wrench is adjusted as tightly as possible against the nut or bolthead before attempting to turn it. D-4-4

Square Drives The square drive (Figure 38), is the female square end, or the end of the socket that attaches to the socket handle. The square drives of sockets range from 14" through 34" sizes are most common. This is standard for both metric and Imperial sockets.

Socket Handles The variety of socket handles picture in Figure 39 all have one thing in common: the holding device that joins the socket handle, and the socket. As you can see, they all have a small, half-exposed ball bearing centred on one side of the square drive and held in place with a bushing just slightly smaller than the bearing. This holding device is known as the friction- ball holding device. D-4-6

Identify Isometric Drawings G-19 Another feature of isometric drawing is the fact that all horizontal and vertical measurements on an orthographic drawing can be transferred directly to an isometric drawing. In other words, an isometric drawing is made using the actual measurements from either the object itself or from an orthographic drawing of it. Figure 14 shows a cube drawn in orthographic projection first and in isometric second. Note that when the cube is sketched in isometric, the sides are still equal in length and have the same measurements as the original cube.

Lines that would not be drawn either vertically or horizontally in orthographic projection — such as angular faces — cannot be drawn on one of the isometric axes. Nor can their angles be established by means of a protractor. In such cases, the lines must be drawn by plotting the points locating their ends and joining these points. See Figure 16. Section lines are used on drawings to show the solid areas of the object that have been cut through. Also, they are often used to indicate the type of material the object is made from. Figure 18 shows some of the more common section lines used, together with their interpretation. Section Views G-37
Section Line Symbols G-38
Figure 19 is an example of a full section. Note that the cutting plane in a full section cuts fully across the object — very often on the centreline of the object if it has one. Front Section A-A

In the previous example of a half section, the centreline is a handy place to stop the section. It is both sensible and practical do this with symmetrical objects like bearings, wheels and tanks. But for some objects a convenient centreline does not exist, so a short break line is used to remove the covering material. Figure 21 shows a broken-out section for a grinding arbor.

Improper storage of fibre ropes can lead to such defects as rot, brittleness, crushed fibres, embedded dirt, kinks and many other defects. Properly stored fibre ropes will give years of trouble-free service. 1. Be sure to coil ropes clockwise. Hang coiled ropes on large diameter pegs in a cool, dry place, where there is good air circulation to prevent mildew. 2. Clean and dry ropes before storing them. Wash ropes with cool water then hang them loosely coiled in a well ventilated area to dry. 3. Stored ropes should be protected from moisture, heat and direct sunlight.
Metal thimble in use

Ropes require very little maintenance other than a thorough cleaning whenever they become soiled. Whipping should be replaced when it shows signs of fraying or loosening. The best form of maintenance is, in fact, careful use. H-2-1

Parts of a Rope H-2-2 The loop in Figure 2 is formed by passing the end of the rope “over” or “in front of” the standing part of the rope. As shown in Figure 3, a loop can also be formed by passing the rope “under” or “behind” the standing part of the rope.

The bowline knot (Figure 4) forms a non-slip loop at the end of a rope. To tie a bowline, begin by forming a small loop by passing the end of the rope over the standing part. Pass the end under the bight and pull it up through the loop. Pass the end behind the standing part, then back down through the loop. Tighten the knot by holding both the end of the rope and the loop in one hand and the standing part in the other hand and pull until the knot is tight.

Bowline Knot To untie the bowline, loosen the knot by pushing the loop which is around the standing part of the rope away from the knot. Once the knot is loosened it is easily untied. The bowline can be used anytime a slip-proof loop is needed. H-2: Identify Eight Knots, Bends and Hitches H-2-3

The half hitch is used for temporarily attaching a rope to an object when the pull will be at right angles to that object. The half hitch is used with other knots to prevent them from coming untied. As illustrated in Figure 5 the rope is passed around the object, then the end is passed around the standing part of the rope. The end is then pinched between the rope and the object being tied.

Half Hitch For safety, the end of the rope must be pinched to the object being secured at a point almost opposite the standing part of the rope. As well, the pull on the standing part of the rope must not be relaxed as this may allow the hitch to come untied. As illustrated in Figure 6, the half hitch is most often tied to the standing part twice, making a secure fastening. It is very important that you make both loops around the standing part in the same direction. If you make one loop clockwise and the other counterclockwise you will find it very difficult to untie the hitch.

The clove hitch is used to secure a rope to a fixed object, such as a post. To tie a clove hitch (Figure 7), take two wraps around the object. The first wrap is made to one side of the standing part and the second wrap must be to the opposite side of the standing part. The end of the rope is then passed between the object and the second wrap. The two wraps are then pulled close to each other and the standing part and the end pulled in opposite directions.
Clove Hitch The clove hitch can be made even more secure by tying the end to the standing part with a single half hitch. H-2: Identify Eight Knots, Bends and Hitches H-2-5
The timber hitch is used to secure a rope to a plank, timber, post or pipe when that object is to be lifted in an upright position as illustrated in Figure 8.

The timber hitch is really just a series of modified half hitches. To tie a timber hitch begin by tying a single half hitch around the object as illustrated in Figure 9. Then pass the free end of the rope between the object and rope two more times as shown in Figure 10. Pull the hitch tight by pulling the standing part of the rope at 90° to the object. Then tie one or more half hitches along the length of the object with the standing part of the rope (Figure 11). H-2-6
